chunks: And from him, from Abu Ja'far, from al-Abbas ibn Ma'ruf, from Hammad ibn Isa, from Aban ibn Uthman, who raised it to Abu Ja'far and Abu Abdillah (peace be upon them both), saying:
The Muhrim (person in Ihram), when he has intercourse with his wife, separation is made between them; meaning by that, they do not be alone unless there is a third person with them.

And when a man has intercourse with his slave-girl while she is in Ihram and he is in Ihram, if he is the one who ordered her to enter Ihram, the expiation is incumbent upon him; and if he is not the one who ordered her to enter Ihram, then there is nothing upon him. Narrated.

key_terms.الْمُحْرِمُ: The person in the state of Ihram (sacred ritual consecration)
key_terms.مُحِلٌّ: One who is not in Ihram (or in the state of Ihram, contextually contrasted)

ai.seo_question: What is the ruling on intimacy for a person in Ihram with their spouse or slave-girl?
ai.summary: This narration from *Tahdhib al-Ahkam* clarifies the distinction between *khalwah* (seclusion) and actual intercourse for a Muhrim, requiring a third party to prevent accidental intimacy. It further delineates the liability of expiation (*kaffarah*) in the case of a slave-girl based on the principle of agency: the master bears the penalty only if he initiated her state of Ihram, reflecting the Shia juristic emphasis on the source of the legal constraint. This highlights the nuanced application of *ta'abbud* (divine command) versus *ta'qil* (rational agency) in ritual purity laws.
